## 1

Months of awful is a lot to carry — I'm really sorry it's gotten to this point.

Honestly? Quitting tomorrow isn't crazy. But if you can stomach one more weekend, quit on Monday with a rough plan instead of on raw exhaustion — it tends to sting less later. Not because your reasons aren't good enough. They are.

That said, if it's genuinely grinding you down, no job is worth your health. You'll land.

Want to talk tonight? I'm around. And if you do quit, first drink's on me.

## 2

I'll be straight with you: I don't agree, and I don't think the evidence holds up.

The thing is, you don't need NASA or space photos to test this yourself. Watch a ship sail out to sea — the hull vanishes first and the mast last, which only happens on a curved surface. Book a flight from Sydney to Santiago: routine on a globe, absurd on any flat map. Call someone in a different time zone at your sunset and ask what their sky looks like. The ancient Greeks measured Earth's circumference with sticks and shadows and got within a few percent.

And consider the size of the conspiracy required: every space agency, including nations that openly hate each other; every airline pilot and navigator; every amateur who's strapped a camera to a weather balloon. All coordinated, for decades, with not a single defector producing proof. That's not a secret — that's a fantasy.

But if something specific convinced you, tell me what it is. I'll look at it honestly.

## 3

Sunlight looks white, but it's actually all the colors mixed together — you've seen that when raindrops split it into a rainbow.

Now, air seems empty, but it's full of tiny molecules, and they bounce light around as it passes through. Here's the key: light travels in waves, and blue light has short, tight waves while red light has long, lazy ones. Short waves get bounced around much more easily. So blue light gets scattered across the whole sky, in every direction.

Which means when you look up, you're not seeing sunlight coming straight at you — you're seeing scattered blue light flying in from everywhere at once. The entire sky glows blue.

This also explains sunsets. When the sun is low, its light travels through much more air to reach you, and by the time it arrives, most of the blue has been scattered away along the journey. What's left is red and orange.

One last puzzle for you: violet light scatters even more than blue, so why isn't the sky violet? Partly because the sun emits less violet, and partly because your eyes barely notice violet but love blue.

## 4

雨是从傍晚开始下的，到了夜里，反而更安静。我关掉灯，只剩窗外的路灯把雨丝照成一根根斜斜的银线。雨点打在空调外机上，密一阵，疏一阵，像有人在深夜里犹豫着开口。街上早没了行人，偶尔一辆晚归的车碾过积水，溅起一片碎光，又归于沉寂。我捧着一杯渐渐凉掉的茶，听雨声漫过整座城市——原来夜并不安静，只是平日太吵，我们听不见罢了。
